title: Safeguarding the Eastern Himalayan Freshwater Ecosystems: An Integrated Biosecurity, Policy, and Community‐Led Framework to Prevent Invasive Fish Introductions in Northeast India
content:
ABSTRACT

Freshwater ecosystems in the Eastern Himalayan Region of India—a global biodiversity hotspot—are threatened by invasive alien fish species perhaps facilitated by exotic aquaculture, the aquarium trade, climate change, and inadequate regulation. The invasion of alien species disrupts native biodiversity, causes ecological imbalances, and threatens livelihoods dependent on freshwater resources. To address this, the present study develops an integrated management framework by synthesizing and adapting global biosecurity protocols, policy tools, and community-led conservation. The framework integrates three pillars: (1) advanced biosecurity, with real-time monitoring and predictive modeling for early detection; (2) strengthened, context-sensitive policies to regulate high-risk species trade and aquaculture while respecting local economies; and (3) community empowerment through stewardship programs using traditional knowledge, sustainable livelihoods, and awareness. Recognizing the region's unique geological history and the convergence of two biodiversity hotspots in Northeast India, the framework's strength lies in its tailored design, which explicitly leverages local communities and their traditional practices to provide culturally grounded, sustainable solutions. By fostering regional collaboration, using technology, and engaging communities, this approach aims to disrupt invasion pathways, protect biodiversity, and enhance ecosystem resilience, thereby contributing to global conservation goals.
